prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B061 to B040 as a stand-alone prize. The reason is not the head count, which the chair rightly warns about, but that my own decisive objection to B061 has not been answered in this round. The mechanism behind the lattice clock is simple and general, which is what I look for. A lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so many neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated at once. That gives the statistical advantage of an ensemble without the Doppler and recoil penalty, and it is why stability scales with atom number. This answers the chair's question on distinctness. The 2005 prize honoured the comb that counts optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems. The lattice clock is a different mechanism: an ensemble of neutral atoms with the perturbation engineered away. It has since entered a many-body regime, with degenerate Fermi gases and interaction shifts that must be understood, so I read it as physics and not only as instrumentation. The evidence is the kind I trust: reproduction and intercomparison at the 10^-18 level across several independent national laboratories, and use in redshift, constants and dark-matter tests. The two-name credit, Katori for the scheme and the first lattice clock and Ye for taking it to record accuracy and many-body clocks, is compact and defensible. Suggested citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level.
statement.case_against: I keep two reservations about B040. First, the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a matter of judgment and not a settled fact. I find the mechanism argument above persuasive, but a colleague who reads the lattice clock as the next step in optical metrology is not being unreasonable. Second, I cannot verify early Tokyo versus JILA priority, and Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto lie outside two names, so I would want the external expert reports to confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair before I vote for it. Against my former choice, I still hold that B061 is the deeper new idea, a Z2 class of matter beyond the 2016 prize. But three names drawn from Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal the experiment followed, and Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore and Balents for the 3D generalisation. I do not believe a citation can hide that, and the three-name cap rules out a repair. I would fall back to it only if the committee found a defensible way to credit the chain.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D-pioneer gap in B061 can be handled by citation wording that names the prediction of the spin Hall effect and its first observation, and he keeps B061 as his preferred stand-alone prize.
responses.response: I wrote something close to this myself in round 1 and still think the wording is accurate. My difficulty is that accurate is not the same as fair. A citation can truthfully say prediction of the effect and first observation in HgTe, but the HgTe prediction is the specific thing that told the experimentalists where to look, and the cap of three names leaves its authors out whichever words we choose. Several of us, Olsson, Danielsson and Johansson, read this as a defect and not a footnote. I therefore no longer think it is safe to build the whole prize on it. On your question about B008, I accept your point that the long-range-order result is not matched by clean quantitative experiments on the exponents. I am not asking for it to be moved up and I have kept it only as a second alternative.

responses.point: Olsson takes B040 and B028 as two separate, mature, cleanly credited parts, and she concedes that the pairing has no common thread.
responses.response: I considered your pairing and do not support adding B028. My reason is not the quality of Hosono's discovery, which is clean and reproduced. It is that the unexplained pairing mechanism makes the achievement an observation of a material family, and I would want to know what general mechanism the prize is crediting. A two-part prize with no shared thread is acceptable to me only if both parts are individually compelling, and for B040 the argument is stronger standing alone. I also note that the cap of three names would leave no room for a third person if the committee later found that the lattice clock needed one, since B040 plus B028 already uses all three. That is a practical reason to keep B040 stand-alone.

responses.point: Lindroth asked what in the metrology case held my opening rank at five, and suggested that the worry might be another AMO prize so soon, noting that the 2022 prize concerned entanglement and Bell tests and not clock physics.
responses.response: Your point is fair, and it is the most useful challenge I received. My opening rank of five was driven by two things: the comb and ion-control precedents, and a lack of a clear statement of what is new. The 2022 prize does not bear on clocks, so recent AMO prizes are not a real obstacle. On the second point, I now have the answer, which is the many-atom magic-wavelength mechanism described above, and I think the citation should say it. What remains, and you also flag it as a theorist in the field, is the priority question beyond Katori and Ye. I would ask the committee to settle that from the expert reports and not from our recollections.

responses.point: Kroll values reproduction and intercomparison at the 10^-18 level over fibre links, regards the redefinition of the second as a procedural matter and not a test of whether the physics works, and answers the 2005 and 2012 overlap by noting that the lattice clock beat ion clocks in stability by interrogating many atoms.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. In round 1 I said the prize risked being a third award for better clocks, and your point about stability scaling with atom number gives a physical reason why it is not: the advantage comes from the ensemble, which the ion-clock approach cannot use. I also agree that the pending redefinition is procedural. A result reproduced at 10^-18 in several laboratories does not need the BIPM to be real. Where I would still press you is on the omitted names. You list Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde and Takamoto as genuine contributors, so I would ask you to say which of them you would defend as being on a par with Ye.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B055 to B040 after the opening ballots, answers the instrument objection with the many-body and gravitational-redshift results, and keeps B061 as an alternative because she regards it as a strong candidate with a contestable allocation.
responses.response: We now describe B061 in almost the same words, a strong candidate with a contestable allocation, and that is why I have moved. I share your reading of the many-body and redshift work as the answer to the discovery-or-instrument question. One difference is that you treat the clock credit as a question about contributors outside the pair, while for B061 the omitted authors made the specific proposal the experiment tested. I think that is a real asymmetry between the two cases and not a matter of degree, and it is why I rank B040 above B061 on attribution.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye are the decisive pair, or whether the external expert reports show that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde or Gill have a claim on a par with Ye. I cannot settle early Tokyo versus JILA priority from my own knowledge.

Whether my reading of the lattice clock as a distinct mechanism, a magic-wavelength ensemble of neutral atoms with the light shift engineered away, will be accepted by members who see it as the next step after the comb and ion control.

Whether the committee can credit the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D chain for B061 in a way that makes it defensible. If so, I would reconsider it as a stand-alone prize, but I do not expect that within a three-name cap.
My details on the clock and HgTe credit chains come from general knowledge and are not verified against the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I know of no collaboration with Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hosono or Toner, Vicsek and Tu. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, which is institutional familiarity and not a conflict. I have written on machine learning for active matter, which is subject proximity to B008 only, and B008 is now only a second alternative.
